body:
What Is the CPU?

The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the primary general-purpose processing component of a computer. It executes program instructions and performs operations needed to process data.

The CPU is often called the brain of the computer because it carries out instructions and controls many essential computing operations. This comparison is useful for remembering its role, but the CPU does not independently decide the purpose of a task as a human brain does.

Main Functional Parts of the CPU

At the introductory level, the CPU is explained through the Arithmetic Logic Unit, Control Unit and small internal storage locations called registers.

Arithmetic Logic Unit

The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs arithmetic and logical operations.

Arithmetic operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Logical operations include comparisons such as determining whether one value is greater than another or whether 2 values are equal.

For example, when a computer calculates the total marks obtained by a student, the arithmetic operation is performed through the CPU's processing circuitry.

Control Unit

The Control Unit (CU) directs and coordinates the execution of instructions. It helps determine which operation is required and controls the sequence of activities needed to perform it.

For example, when an instruction requires addition, the control unit directs the processing operation, while the ALU performs the required arithmetic.

The control unit is responsible for coordination rather than carrying out every arithmetic calculation itself.

Registers

Registers are small, extremely fast storage locations within the CPU. They temporarily hold data, instructions or intermediate values needed for immediate processing.

Registers differ from ordinary file storage because they are intended for very short-term use during CPU operations.

How the CPU Processes an Instruction

At a basic level, CPU instruction execution can be understood through 3 activities:

  1. Fetch: The CPU obtains the next instruction from memory.
  2. Decode: The CPU determines which operation the instruction requires.
  3. Execute: The CPU performs the required operation, such as calculation, comparison or transferring information.

These activities are repeated as a program runs. Modern processors can carry out complex sequences of operations, but the basic distinction between obtaining an instruction, interpreting it and executing it remains useful.

Example: Calculating Examination Marks

Suppose an application must calculate the total of 65, 75 and 80.

The application instructions and necessary data are made available in working memory. The CPU obtains the relevant instructions. The control unit coordinates their execution, and the arithmetic processing circuitry performs the additions needed to obtain 220.

The resulting value can then be used by the application and displayed through an output device.

The CPU performs processing, but it does not replace the functions of memory, storage or input and output devices. A CPU alone is not a complete usable computer.

CPU and Operating System: Different Roles

The CPU is physical hardware. The operating system is software that manages computer resources and helps coordinate the execution of applications.

For example, an operating system may arrange CPU time for several active applications. The CPU executes the instructions, while the operating system manages how computing resources are allocated.

Prelims focus

  • CPU stands for Central Processing Unit.
  • ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit.
  • CU stands for Control Unit.
  • The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
  • The Control Unit coordinates instruction execution.
  • Trap: The ALU and Control Unit have different functions; neither should be confused with RAM or a storage drive.

[Sources: National Institute of Open Schooling, Data Entry Operations, Lesson 1, section 1.3.1, Computer Organisation, printed pp. 2–3; IBM, What Is a Central Processing Unit?, sections on CPU functions and components; CBSE, Computer Science, Class XI, Unit 1, Chapters 1 and 4, Computer Fundamentals and Microprocessors and Memory Concepts. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Central Processing Unit: Arithmetic, Logic and Control

body:
Why Computers Need Memory and Storage

A computer needs to retain instructions, data and results. Some information must be available very quickly while a program is running, whereas other information must remain available after the computer is switched off.

This explains the distinction between working memory and persistent storage.

Primary Memory

Primary memory refers to memory used closely by the computer's processing system. In introductory textbooks, RAM and ROM are commonly discussed as major forms of primary memory.

Random Access Memory

RAM stands for Random Access Memory. It is the computer's principal working memory for active programs and the data they currently use.

When a user opens an application, the operating system makes the application and its necessary data available in RAM for execution. RAM supports rapid access during active operations.

Ordinary computer RAM is volatile, meaning that its contents are lost when the required electrical power is removed.

For example, information being edited in an application may be present in RAM before it is saved to persistent storage. If power fails, unsaved changes may be lost unless the application has already stored a recoverable copy.

Read-Only Memory

ROM stands for Read-Only Memory. ROM is a form of non-volatile memory, meaning that it retains information without continuous electrical power.

In basic computer education, ROM is associated with instructions needed during system startup. Modern devices may use rewritable non-volatile flash memory for firmware, but the essential distinction from ordinary RAM remains that the stored information persists without power.

ROM or firmware storage is not normally the place where a user saves everyday documents.

Cache Memory

Cache memory is a small, high-speed memory used to keep frequently needed data or instructions close to the processor. It reduces the need for the CPU to retrieve the same information repeatedly from slower working memory.

Cache is generally smaller and faster than main RAM. CPU registers provide even more immediate storage for processing operations.

Secondary Storage

Secondary storage retains files, applications and other information for later use. Common examples include hard disk drives, solid-state drives, USB flash drives and optical discs.

Hard Disk Drive

A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on rotating disks. It provides persistent storage, so saved files remain available after normal shutdown.

Solid-State Drive

A Solid-State Drive (SSD) stores data using electronic memory, commonly flash memory. Unlike a conventional HDD, an SSD does not require spinning magnetic disks.

SSDs generally provide faster access than conventional HDDs, although actual performance depends on the device.

Other Storage Devices

  • USB flash drive: Portable, non-volatile storage used to transfer or retain files.
  • Memory card: Compact non-volatile storage commonly used in cameras and other electronic devices.
  • CD and DVD: Optical storage media that use light-based reading technology.

Comparison of Memory and Storage

ComponentMain useVolatile?Typical role
RAMActive programs and dataYesWorking memory
ROMPersistent instructions or firmwareNoStartup support
CacheFrequently needed processing dataUsually yesHigh-speed access
HDDSaved files and applicationsNoPersistent storage
SSDSaved files and applicationsNoPersistent storage

What Happens When a File Is Saved?

Consider a student editing a document. The application uses RAM while the document is being edited. When the student saves the document, the application and operating system arrange for its data to be written to a storage device such as an SSD.

After shutdown, ordinary RAM contents disappear, but the successfully saved file remains on the SSD. When the file is opened again, the necessary data is read from storage and made available for processing.

Basic Units of Digital Information

A bit is a binary digit that can represent 0 or 1. A byte consists of 8 bits.

Memory and storage capacity are commonly expressed using units such as kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes. These units represent progressively larger quantities of information.

There is an important unit convention: decimal storage units use multiples of 1000, while binary units such as KiB and MiB use multiples of 1024. The difference can explain why storage capacity appears differently in some specifications and computer displays.

RAM is not the same as permanent file storage. RAM supports active work, while devices such as HDDs and SSDs retain successfully saved files after power is removed.

Prelims focus

  • RAM: Random Access Memory; normally volatile working memory.
  • ROM: Read-Only Memory; non-volatile memory.
  • Cache memory: small, high-speed memory used to reduce access delays.
  • HDD: magnetic storage using rotating disks.
  • SSD: non-volatile electronic storage without rotating magnetic disks.
  • 1 byte equals 8 bits.
  • Trap: Increasing RAM capacity does not automatically increase the permanent storage capacity available for saved files.

[Sources: CBSE, Computer Science, Class XI, Unit 1, Chapter 4, Microprocessors and Memory Concepts; IBM, Primary Storage vs. Secondary Storage: What's the Difference?, sections on RAM, ROM, cache and storage; IBM, Hard Disk Drive vs. Solid-State Drive: What's the Difference?, sections on HDD and SSD functions. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Power loss may erase unsaved changes in volatile RAM, while a document successfully saved to an SSD remains and can be reopened after restart.
pictures.caption: RAM holds active work, while persistent storage retains successfully saved files.

title: Computer Memory and Storage: RAM, ROM, Cache, HDD and SSD

body:
Input Devices

An input device allows data or instructions to enter a computer. Input may consist of typed characters, pointer movements, images, audio, scanned marks or other information.

Keyboard

A keyboard is primarily used to enter text, numbers and commands. It contains different groups of keys, including alphabetic keys, numeric keys, function keys and control keys.

Mouse and Other Pointing Devices

A mouse controls a pointer and allows users to select items through clicking and other actions.

A trackball is another pointing device. Instead of moving the complete device across a surface, the user rotates a ball to control pointer movement.

A touchpad detects finger movement and is commonly provided on laptops.

Scanner

A scanner captures information from a physical document or image and converts it into digital form. The resulting scan may be stored as an image or processed further by software.

Microphone and Camera

A microphone captures sound as input. A digital camera or webcam supplies image or video input.

Speech recognition software may process microphone input and convert spoken words into text. The microphone is the input hardware, while the recognition process is performed by software.

Touchscreen

A touchscreen allows users to select items or enter commands by touching the displayed interface.

A touchscreen combines 2 functions: its display presents visual output, while its touch-sensing system receives user input.

Special Input Technologies

Some input technologies are particularly useful for reading printed documents, examination forms and bank instruments.

Optical Character Recognition

OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition. OCR technology identifies printed or other supported text in an image and converts it into machine-readable character data.

For example, a scanned printed page can be processed using OCR software to obtain text that may be searched or edited. A scanner captures the image; OCR performs character recognition.

Optical Mark Recognition

OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition. It identifies marks placed in predefined positions on a form.

OMR is commonly used to process multiple-choice answer sheets and questionnaires. It detects marked response positions rather than generally interpreting complete sentences as ordinary text.

Magnetic Ink Character Recognition

MICR stands for Magnetic Ink Character Recognition. It recognises specially printed characters that use magnetic ink.

MICR is associated particularly with cheque processing in banking. It is different from OCR because it is designed to recognise characters printed using magnetic ink and suitable character formats.

TechnologyRecognisesTypical application
OCRCharacters from document imagesConverting scanned text into editable text
OMRMarks in predefined positionsObjective examination answer sheets
MICRSpecial magnetic-ink charactersBank cheque processing

Output Devices

An output device presents processed information in a form that a person or another receiving system can use.

Monitor

A monitor displays text, images, videos and other visual information. Modern monitors commonly use flat-panel display technology.

Information displayed electronically on a screen is an example of soft copy.

Printer

A printer produces information on physical media such as paper. The resulting printed document is called a hard copy.

Common printer types include:

  • Dot-matrix printer: An impact printer that produces characters or images using pins striking an inked ribbon.
  • Inkjet printer: A non-impact printer that deposits small droplets of ink.
  • Laser printer: A non-impact printer that commonly uses toner to produce printed output.

The distinction between impact and non-impact printers concerns whether printing involves mechanically striking an inked ribbon against the printing surface.

Speaker and Headphones

Speakers and headphones provide audio output. They can reproduce music, speech, notifications and other sounds. Spoken output can also support accessibility for users who cannot easily read visual information.

Projector and Plotter

A projector displays visual output on a larger surface. A plotter is used for producing drawings and other graphical output, particularly where specialised plotting capabilities are required.

Devices That Perform More Than One Function

Some computer devices cannot be classified as exclusively input or exclusively output.

  • Touchscreen: Receives touch input and presents visual output.
  • Multifunction printer: May scan documents as input and print documents as output.
  • Communication interface: Can send and receive information, although communication functions are distinct from ordinary user input and output examples.

A device's classification depends on what it does. For example, a monitor displays output, whereas the touch-sensing function of a touchscreen provides input. Combining them in one product does not make their individual functions identical.

Prelims focus

  • Keyboard, mouse, scanner and microphone are input devices.
  • Monitor, printer, speaker and projector are output devices.
  • A touchscreen provides both input and output.
  • OCR recognises characters; OMR recognises marked positions; MICR recognises magnetic-ink characters.
  • A printer produces hard copy; a monitor normally presents soft copy.
  • Trap: Scanning a document creates a digital image, but OCR is needed when its characters must be recognised as editable text.

[Sources: National Institute of Open Schooling, Data Entry Operations, Lesson 1, sections 1.5 and 1.6, Input Devices and Output Devices, printed pp. 4–10; CBSE, Installation Technician: Computing and Peripherals, Class XI, Chapter 3, Input and Output Devices, printed pp. 47–65; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 16, Light, printed p. 209, section on assistive electronic aids. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
